transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you into the clinic today?

Well, I'm here... I suppose I'm here because things at work have gotten completely out of hand, and honestly, I don't know who else to talk to about it. I work in mathematical sciences, specifically environmental modeling, and I've been leading this major contract. It's a massive undertaking, lots of moving parts, lots of data. But recently, well, not just recently, it's been going on for a while now, I'm pretty sure—no, I'm certain—that the people on this contract, the ones who are supposed to be collaborating with me, have been tracking every single revision I make. 

And it's not just tracking, they are actively planting errors in the datasets. I'll run the models, the math is solid, I check it three, four times, and then suddenly, there's a discrepancy. A glaring error that I know I didn't make. They're doing it to make it look like I'm incompetent, like I can't lead the work anymore. They want me out. 

I've tried explaining this. I sat down with my wife just the other night, laid out all the logs, showed her the timestamps, but she just keeps saying it's version-control mistakes. The junior analysts say the same thing—"Oh, it's just a git merge issue," or "Someone overwrote the file by accident." But that's statistically impossible given the frequency and the specific nature of these errors! It's targeted. It's deliberate sabotage, and no one seems to understand the gravity of what they're doing to my data, to my reputation... it's exhausting, frankly, having to constantly defend my own calculations against this kind of coordinated interference.
Have you ever heard voices, whispering, or other sounds when no one else was around?

Voices? No, no, I don't... I don't hear voices or whispers or anything like that. I'm a man of science, Doctor, a mathematician. I deal in hard facts, in empirical evidence and concrete data. If I were sitting around hearing phantom voices when no one was there, well, I'd be the first to admit that something was neurologically amiss and I'd go get a brain scan. 

But that's not what this is. I don't hear whispers in the empty room. What I do see, however, is the silent, insidious manipulation of my work. It's not in my head, it's on the screen. Just last Thursday, for example, I was in my office—perfectly quiet, just the hum of the ventilation system, absolutely no one around, no sounds at all—and I'm watching the terminal, and the parameters for the aquifer depletion model just... change. Right there. The variables shifted. 

So, no, I'm not hearing things. The only thing speaking to me, if you want to use a metaphor, are the server logs, and they are telling me very clearly that someone is logging in remotely and sabotaging the variables. I don't need to hear voices to know I'm being targeted, the math proves it. It's all right there in the code, plain as day, if anyone would just take the time to actually look at the standard deviations with me instead of asking if I'm hearing ghosts.
Have you ever felt like an outside force or someone else was controlling your thoughts, feelings, or actions?

Controlling my thoughts? No, no, absolutely not. My mind is entirely my own. I mean, think about it logically—if someone or something were controlling my thoughts or my actions, I wouldn't be able to catch the errors they're planting in the code, would I? No, my cognitive faculties are strictly under my own jurisdiction. 

You see, Doctor, when you spend decades—I'm sixty years old, and I've been doing this kind of rigorous analytical work since I first took advanced statistics back in college—when you spend that much time honing your intellect, your mind becomes a very structured, very secure environment. It has to be. Environmental modeling requires an immense amount of focus. You have to hold complex, multi-variable equations in your head, balancing fluid dynamics with thermal decay rates, and you simply cannot do that if you aren't in complete, absolute control of your own mental processes. 

So, no, nobody is beaming thoughts into my head or making me move my hands like a marionette. That's science fiction. What's happening to me is grounded in reality. The outside force isn't in my head, it's in the network architecture. They can't touch my thoughts, so they go after the one thing they *can* access, which is the shared drive. They know my mind is sharp. They know I can see right through their little version-control excuses. Honestly, if they could control my thoughts, they would just make me think the errors were my own fault! They would just make me feel incompetent so I'd step down quietly. But they can't do that. I know what I calculated. I know the standard deviations I set. 

I feel perfectly in control of my own emotions and actions, even if I am understandably frustrated—deeply, deeply frustrated—by this whole ordeal. It's just... it's insulting, really, to think that my own mind would be compromised when it's the external variables, the actual tangible data, that's being manipulated by these people. My thoughts are my own. Always have been.
Outside of this situation at work, have you generally found it difficult throughout your life to trust other people?

Difficult to trust? No... no, I wouldn't say that at all. In fact, quite the opposite, really. I mean, if you look at my track record, the very nature of my career—environmental modeling on a macro scale—it absolutely demands trust. You simply cannot build a comprehensive model of, say, regional watershed dynamics without relying on a vast network of other people's data. For decades, I’ve worked with hydrologists, field researchers, junior analysts... and I’ve always trusted them. When a colleague hands me a dataset on soil saturation, I don't assume they've doctored the numbers. I take it at face value, because in the mathematical sciences, you operate on a baseline of professional integrity. 

Even going back to my days in college, I was always putting together study groups, sharing notes, collaborating on complex proofs. I’ve never been the sort of person who looks over his shoulder or thinks the neighbors are going through my mail or anything absurd like that. That’s just not who I am. I’m a pragmatist. I trust my wife implicitly, for instance, even if she is currently failing to grasp the technical severity of what I'm showing her on those server logs. My personal relationships have always been perfectly fine.

Honestly, Doctor, that is exactly why this current situation at work is so profoundly disturbing to me. If I were a naturally suspicious person, a... a cynic, I suppose, maybe I would have seen this coordinated effort coming much sooner. But I went into this major contract with complete, unshakeable faith in my collaborators. I authorized shared administrative access to the repositories without a single second thought, because that is standard operating procedure. You trust your team. It wasn't until the math stopped aligning—until the discrepancies in the code became so statistically improbable that they could only be the result of deliberate human interference—that I was forced to reevaluate what was happening right in front of me. 

So, no, I don't have some lifelong psychological issue with trusting people. I have a very current, very specific issue with a group of people who are actively exploiting the professional trust I gave them in order to ruin my data.
